text: exercise: gain additional experience and knowledge of using the AMEC process in an expeditionary environment and demonstrate knowledge transfer of the AMEC and foundry processes to enlisted military personnel. At the exercise, the aluminum furnace was used, and various components were investment cast including bilge plugs, wrenches, manifolds, and mounting brackets. Several military members were able to be trained and achieve proficiency such that they could conduct the entire process without support from ORNL staff. The exercise was very successful. Pictures from the exercise cannot be shared at this time. 1.2.4 Material Characterization and Qualification Data Material characterization and qualification is critical for all manufacturing processes. If a manufactured component can’t meet the required properties, it will fail in its operational environment. Regulated industries such as aerospace, energy, and defense have strict guidelines on material and component performance that must be met for a part to be certified. Because the AMEC process is very comparable to lost foam casting, with the resultant part being a casting made by pouring molten metal similar to any other casting process, the resultant material properties are very comparable. This was initially conducted by Skuld when developing the AMEC process. Now, more scrutinous testing and review is needed to characterize and qualify the materials with more thorough datasets that can be provided to potential partners. To do this, Skuld manufactured a variety of samples to be sent to an independent testing lab for verification. These samples included square and round tensile testing bars. Collected data includes tensile strength, yield strength, elongation in 4D, area location, and fracture location. A summary of the test results can be seen in Table 1. The full datasets from the reports generated by NSL Analytical, an independent testing laboratory in Cleveland, Ohio, are attached in the appendix of this report. Because AMEC is a casting process, materials are easily qualified and can use establish properties for cast components. This greatly shortens the qualification time in comparison to metal components made entirely with additive manufacturing. Further expansion and distribution of the AMEC process will help recover the foundry industry in America. Reports suggest that a large majority of American foundries have closed in the last century, including more than a third of steel foundries closing since 2000. Most foundry work has gone offshore, but the AMEC process shows potential to reshore foundry capabilities. This project and the opportunities through Innovation Crossroads have also been impactful for Skuld.
